2.note: The word translated as **summer fruit** sounds very much like the word for **end**. Yahweh’s purpose in showing Amos summer fruit was to give him a prophecy of the end of his people. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.
See how you translated this same phrase in 7:8.

3.note: Here, **the songs of the temple** represents “the people who sing the songs in the temple.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the singers in the temple will wail]

The phrase **in that day** refers to that time when Yahweh will punish them, also referred to as “the day of Yahweh” in chapter 5. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at the time when I punish you]

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words here, is interjecting **the declaration of the Lord Yahweh** to emphasize that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

Yahweh is using a word that expresses a strong feeling of dread. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Say nothing, for the dread is too great]
The pronoun **one** does not refer to any particular person. It refers to people in general. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [people have thrown]

4.note: Amos is speaking of these people oppressing needy people as if they were **trampling** them underfoot. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones oppressing the needy]

Amos is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are needy people]

By **cause the afflicted of the land to cease**, Amos means that they brought about the ruin of the poor because of their unfair treatment which **afflicted** them. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and bring to ruin the afflicted of the land]

Amos is using the adjective **afflicted** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the afflicted people of the land]

5.q: מָתַ֞י יַעֲבֹ֤ר הַ⁠חֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ וְ⁠נַשְׁבִּ֣ירָה שֶּׁ֔בֶר וְ⁠הַ⁠שַּׁבָּ֖ת וְ⁠נִפְתְּחָה־בָּ֑ר
5.note: The implication is that the Israelites were not permitted to buy and sell on the festival of **the new moon** or on **the Sabbath**, and so these merchants were impatient for those days to end. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When will the new moon festival, on which we are not allowed to trade, be over, so that we may sell grain, and when will the Sabbath, on which we are also forbidden to trade, be over, so that we may open our bins of wheat]

The implication is that these merchants would measure out grain in a container smaller than a standard **ephah** and weigh their customers’ silver with a weight heavier than a standard **shekel**, so that they cheated the people who bought from them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to use an undersized ephah measure for grain and an oversized shekel weight for silver]

Amos is using the possessive form to describe **balances** that are characterized by **deceit**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [deceitful balances]

6.q: לִ⁠קְנ֤וֹת בַּ⁠כֶּ֨סֶף֙ דַּלִּ֔ים וְ⁠אֶבְי֖וֹן בַּ⁠עֲב֣וּר נַעֲלָ֑יִם
6.note: The merchants are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to buy the poor as slaves with silver and to buy the needy as slaves in exchange for a pair of sandals]

The merchants are using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [poor people with silver and needy people]

The implication is that **a pair of sandals** would only cost a very small amount. This means that they were buying needy people as slaves for a price as low as the price of a pair of sandals. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the needy for as little as the price of a pair of sandals]

7.note: As in 6:8, **the pride of Jacob** could refer to: (1) the land of Israel, since that is its meaning elsewhere, and it would make no sense to swear by something negative, such as sinful pride. Alternate translation: [by this land that Jacob’s people are so proud of] or (2) Yahweh himself. This would then be equivalent to the phrase in 6:8, “The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his soul.” Alternate translation: [by himself, of whom Jacob’s people are so proud]

Here, **Jacob** represents the descendants of Jacob, the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Jacob’s descendants]

Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”), which would be the penalty for not telling the truth. Normally the penalty would be understood to be something general such as “may Yahweh punish me severely,” yielding something like, “If I ever forget…, then may Yahweh punish me severely…” But since Yahweh is speaking, stating this would not make sense. It may be clearest to translate the oath as a positive statement, as in the UST.

8.q: הַ֤⁠עַל זֹאת֙ לֹֽא־תִרְגַּ֣ז הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠אָבַ֖ל כָּל־יוֹשֵׁ֣ב בָּ֑⁠הּ
8.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the land will certainly tremble and that everyone living in it will certainly mourn. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The land will surely tremble over this, and everyone dwelling in it will mourn!]

The pronoun **this** refers to the deeds of the people that Yahweh mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will not the land tremble over the evil deeds that the people have done]

8.q: וְ⁠עָלְתָ֤ה כָ⁠אֹר֙ כֻּלָּ֔⁠הּ וְ⁠נִגְרְשָׁ֥ה ו⁠נשקה כִּ⁠יא֥וֹר מִצְרָֽיִם
8.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the Nile of Egypt** rises in flood and then sinks back down again, so the whole land of Israel will heave up and down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And the whole land will heave upward and then settle back down, just as the Nile of Egypt rises in flood and then recedes]

9.note: The phrase **in that day** refers to that time when Yahweh will punish them. See how you translated this same phrase in verse 3.

Amos, who is conveying Yahweh’s words here, is interjecting **the declaration of the Lord** to emphasize that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

9.q: וְ⁠הֵבֵאתִ֥י הַ⁠שֶּׁ֖מֶשׁ בַּֽ⁠צָּהֳרָ֑יִם וְ⁠הַחֲשַׁכְתִּ֥י לָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ בְּ⁠י֥וֹם אֽוֹר
9.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional as in the UST. Another approach would be to combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [that I will make the sunlight completely disappear in the middle of the day]

10.note: Wearing **sackcloth** and shaving the head were a symbolic actions by which Yahweh’s people would show that they were mourning and grieving. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And I will cause everyone to put on sackcloth around their waists and to shave their heads bald to show their grief]

10.q: וְ⁠שַׂמְתִּ֨י⁠הָ֙ כְּ⁠אֵ֣בֶל יָחִ֔יד וְ⁠אַחֲרִיתָ֖⁠הּ כְּ⁠י֥וֹם מָֽר
10.note: The point of these comparisons is that just as the death of an **only child** brings parents the deepest possible grief, and just as **a bitter day** brings the greatest sorrow, so the people of Israel will grieve when Yahweh punishes them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And I will cause you to grieve as deeply as parents who mourn the death of their only child, and everything will end in the most bitter sorrow]

11.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention, for]

Amos is interjecting the phrase **the declaration of the Lord Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

11.q: רָעָ֖ב בָּ⁠אָ֑רֶץ לֹֽא־רָעָ֤ב לַ⁠לֶּ֨חֶם֙ וְ⁠לֹֽא־צָמָ֣א לַ⁠מַּ֔יִם כִּ֣י אִם־לִ⁠שְׁמֹ֔עַ אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
11.note: Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [it will not be a famine for food and it will not be a thirst for water, but rather I will send a thirst to hear the words of Yahweh]

12.note: Yahweh is referring to all of the land by naming the extremes, **from sea to sea** and **from the north and to the sunrise**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in every direction throughout the whole land]
Here, **the sunrise** represents “east.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

13.note: See how you translated the same phrase, “in that day,” in verse 3. Alternate translation: [At the time when I punish you]

Yahweh is using **the beautiful virgins** and **the young men**, to represent the strongest and healthiest of the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [even the strongest among the people, will faint]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the young men will faint from thirst]

14.note: Here, **the guilt of Samaria** represents the sin of idolatry practiced by the people there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by the idolatry in Samaria that made the people guilty]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **guilt**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by what makes Samaria guilty]

14.q: וְ⁠אָמְר֗וּ חֵ֤י אֱלֹהֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ דָּ֔ן וְ⁠חֵ֖י דֶּ֣רֶךְ בְּאֵֽר־שָׁ֑בַע
14.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation as modeled in the UST.

Following the custom of the culture, these people are swearing an oath by naming something that they hold sacred when they say **By the life of your god, Dan**. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [As surely as your god lives, Dan]

Here, **by the life of the way of Beersheba** represents the god that people traveled to worship at Beersheba. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and, ‘As surely as the god lives that people go on pilgrimage to worship at Beersheba]

Yahweh is speaking of these people being destroyed with no hope of recovery as if they would **fall** down and never **rise** again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will be destroyed, and they will never recover]
